extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, entomologists, and evolutionary_biologists (scientifically literate readers interested in sexual selection)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence used to infer sexual selection (and its mechanisms) in insects, including morphology, behaviour, ontogeny, fossil record, variability, and comparisons between sexes and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of differentiation/specialisation of sexual organ (musical apparatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the musical apparatus is more differentiated or specialised in the Locustidae ... than in the Achetidae" — degree of specialisation of sound-producing organs indicates importance in mating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats greater structural differentiation (e.g. specialised bow and fiddle wings, talc-like plates, speculum) as evidence that the organ has been enhanced by sexual selection for calling or alluring females. Examples: Locustidae have more specialised apparatus and are 'the most powerful performers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural derivation from pre-existing parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures (e.g. teeth on wing nervures) appear to have been "developed by the aid of selection, from the minute scales and hairs" — evidence that ornaments/structures evolved by modification of earlier features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of intermediate or derivable structures supports an origin by selection rather than sudden creation; cited examples include teeth of nervures and coleopteran structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of direct stimulus/use (friction) in development
rubrics_metrics.description: Development may be "in part directly due to the stimulus from the friction of one wing over the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that some features can be promoted both by sexual selection and by direct mechanical stimulation (use/disuse), so absence of full independence from use does not preclude sexual selection. Example: development of wing teeth partly due to friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour / asymmetry as evidence of specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiation of paired structures (one wing acting as bow, the other as fiddle) implies gradual specialization on the "principle of the division of labour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formerly similar paired structures become asymmetric and take distinct roles, this pattern is taken as evidence of adaptive specialization (likely through selection). Example: Locustidae vs. Achetidae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification of accidental useful variation
rubrics_metrics.description: A grating sound "occasionally and accidentally made by the males ... might readily have been intensified through sexual selection, by variations in the roughness of the nervures having been continually preserved."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small accidental behaviours or structures that incidentally attract mates can be amplified by sexual selection; use as a causal mechanism for origin of mating signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of rudimentary structures in females
rubrics_metrics.description: Females are "almost always destitute of an efficient musical apparatus," but often have rudiments of male organs; this pattern informs hypotheses about transfer or independent development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurrence of reduced or rudimentary versions of male traits in females may indicate (a) inheritance from males, (b) past transfer from males to females, or (c) independent but functionless development; Darwin uses such observations to infer evolutionary history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogenetic timing of development (maturation-linked growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Acridiidae the stridulating teeth in males "become further developed, and acquire their perfect structure at the last moult, when the insect is mature and ready to breed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits that develop or are enhanced at sexual maturity strongly suggest sexual selection acting on breeding success rather than on juvenile survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent diversity of mechanisms achieving same function
rubrics_metrics.description: "Throughout the animal kingdom we often find the same object gained by the most diversified means" — different morphological solutions for producing sound indicate high adaptive importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When unrelated groups evolve widely different mechanisms to achieve the same mating-related function (e.g., sound-production), this convergence/diversity supports a strong selective pressure for that function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fossil evidence indicating long time for evolution of mating structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a fossil insect in the Devonian "which is furnished with 'the well-known tympanum or stridulating apparatus'" shows "there has been more than ample time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of mating-related structures in ancient fossils supports gradual evolution over long periods, strengthening selection-based explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in colouration as indicator of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where sexes often differ in colour (e.g. Libellulidae), bright male colours are considered by observers (MacLachlan) to "serve as a sexual attraction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent and conspicuous differences in colour between sexes, especially when correlated with mating behaviour or colour attraction experiments, are taken as evidence for sexual selection. Counter-examples where sexes do not differ weaken sexual-selection explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanations for conspicuous coloration (aposematism/recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright tints "may be of use ... by giving notice that they are unpalatable"; similarly colors may serve recognition rather than attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin repeatedly cautions that conspicuous colours may function as warning coloration or for crypsis/recognition; such alternative functions must be considered before attributing ornamentation to sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural evidence: male-male combat and contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed fighting or "pugnacious" behaviour among males (e.g. crickets, mantids, some beetles) supports the idea that structures (mandibles, horns) function in contests for females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct observation of males fighting for females, or behaviourally contesting access, is strong evidence for male-male competition driving the evolution of weapons and related traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-specific development and transfer of traits across sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits "gained by one sex through sexual selection have often been transferred in a variable degree to the other sex," e.g., pollen-collecting apparatus transmitted to males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that characters originating in one sex can be partially or wholly expressed in the other; this must be accounted for when inferring origin and function of traits in either sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population/sex-ratio and mating system context
rubrics_metrics.description: In bees, "the males search eagerly and fight ... In some cases the males are far more numerous than the females," which can influence sexual selection dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecological/demographic context (e.g., skewed sex ratios, male abundance, mating system) is used as evidence to infer the intensity and direction of sexual selection (e.g., female choice vs. male competition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability (extreme individual variation) as indicator of ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Horns are "remarkable from their excessive variability; so that a graduated series can be formed ..." Darwin infers that extreme variability and diversity among closely related species indicate ornamental function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High variability of a trait within a species, and rapid divergence among related species, argue against a fixed utilitarian function and for sexual selection as an explanatory mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of wear/friction marks argues against functional use
rubrics_metrics.description: The horns "do not shew marks of friction, as if used for any ordinary work," undermining hypotheses of utilitarian function (e.g., defence or burrowing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural absence of use-related wear or lack of mechanical suitability reduces the plausibility of a trait being adaptive for ordinary tasks and supports ornament/sexual-display hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and morphological trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of certain horns "may have been caused through the principle of compensation, owing to the development of the large horns and projections on the lower surface;" also female rudiments described as results of compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphological loss or reduction in one region concurrent with elaboration elsewhere (compensation) can explain absence of expected structures and must be considered when reconstructing evolutionary pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimorphism within males (two male morphs) indicates alternative strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: In Siagonium and Bledius some males form two sets differing greatly in horn/body size without intermediates; this suggests strict dimorphism and alternative male forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of distinct male morphs with different weaponry/size suggests multiple mating strategies (e.g., fighter vs. sneaker), which is an important dimension of sexual selection analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of morphological features with mating-related function (clinging, holding during copulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Projections on anterior femora and forked horns (Onitis furcifer) "may aid the male in clinging to the female."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphological structures plausibly aiding courtship or copulation (e.g., grasping appendages) should be evaluated for functional correlation with mating behaviour; such plausible function supports sexual-selection interpretations.
